title: Manager Effectiveness Scorecard: Metrics, Targets and Benchmarks
summary: A manager effectiveness scorecard: which metrics to track, an example layout, how to set targets from your own baseline, and how to run monthly reviews.
body_markdown:
**TLDR:** A manager effectiveness scorecard tracks how each manager supports their team, one measure at a time. What to know:


- Put **5 to 10 measures** side by side: 1:1s, meeting load, focus time, after-hours messages and links to other teams.
- Keep the measures **separate** . One blended score hides which habit needs work.
- Set targets from **your own baseline** first: the organization median, quarters and trends.
- Add **outside benchmarks** only from data you can trace, split by role.
- Review it **monthly with each manager** and use it for coaching, not ranking.


Your engagement survey says one team is struggling, but not why. Its manager says the team is fine. A scorecard built from how the team actually spends its week shows what is behind the survey result: 1:1s that keep getting cancelled, a calendar with no time to focus or messages that arrive late every night.


This guide lists the metrics for a manager effectiveness scorecard, shows an example layout, and explains how to set targets, use benchmarks and run reviews.


## What a manager effectiveness scorecard is, and why it beats a single score


A manager effectiveness scorecard is a short set of measures, shown side by side for each team, that tracks how a manager supports the team week to week. Manager effectiveness has several parts, and a single blended score hides which part needs work. A scorecard keeps the measures separate, so a manager can see, for example, that 1:1s are steady but the team's focus time is shrinking.


Surveys tell you that a team is struggling. A scorecard built from work patterns helps explain why, and it updates every week instead of once a year.


## The five habits the scorecard tracks


The metrics below map to five manager habits, explained in depth in our post on[manager effectiveness metrics that matter more than eSat scores](https://www.worklytics.co/blog/manager-effectiveness-5-metrics-that-matter-more-than-esat-scores) :


- **Coach regularly.** Hold 1:1s and keep them.
- **Set reasonable team norms.** Protect focus time and avoid pressure after hours.
- **Support without micromanaging.** Be present in the team's work, but not in every meeting.
- **Connect the team.** Link the team to other groups and to senior leaders.
- **Spend time together in person** where the team works in an office.


Google's[Project Oxygen](https://rework.withgoogle.com/intl/en/guides/following-the-data-the-research-behind-great-managers) reached a similar list. Google analyzed over 10,000 data points about its managers and found 10 behaviors of highly effective managers, including being a good coach, empowering the team without micromanaging and collaborating across the company.


## The metrics on the scorecard


Each metric is calculated per team, over a week or 4 weeks, from data most companies already have. Reporting lines from the HR system matter: without them you cannot tell a manager's 1:1 from any other 1:1.


Metric Habit How to calculate (per team, per week or 4 weeks) Data source


Manager 1:1s per direct report Coaching 1:1 meetings between the manager and each direct report, averaged across the team Calendar and HR system


Cancelled 1:1s Coaching Scheduled manager 1:1s that were cancelled Calendar


Weeks since last 1:1 Coaching Weeks since each direct report's last 1:1 with their manager Calendar and HR system


Share of meeting hours with the manager present Support without micromanaging Share of team members' meeting hours that their manager also attends Calendar and HR system


Manager-started share of collaboration Support without micromanaging Of the time a manager and a report spend collaborating, the share the manager started Calendar, email, chat


After-hours chat messages from the manager Team norms Chat messages the team receives from their manager outside working hours Slack, Microsoft Teams, Google Chat


Team meeting hours and recurring meeting hours Team norms Total and recurring meeting hours per team member Calendar


Focus hours and fragmented hours Team norms Hours in uninterrupted blocks of 2 hours or more, compared with hours broken into shorter pieces Calendar, email, chat


Collaboration with other groups Connection Share of the team's collaboration time spent with people in other groups Calendar, email, chat and HR system


Skip-level co-attendance Connection Share of meeting hours where the manager's own manager is also present Calendar and HR system


Span of control Capacity Direct reports, split into individual contributors and managers HR system


Retention and engagement Outcome Regretted attrition by team, engagement or upward feedback scores HR system, surveys


Start with five or six of these, not all twelve. Add more once managers trust the first ones.


## Example scorecard layout


One row per metric for each team, with the organization median for context and the trend over the last 12 weeks. The numbers below are made up, and the flags are examples to adapt, not industry benchmarks.


Metric Team value Org median Trend (last 12 weeks) Example flag


Manager 1:1s per direct report (4 weeks) 3.0 2.5 Steady Fewer than 2


Cancelled 1:1s (4 weeks) 1 1 Steady More than 2


Share of meeting hours with the manager present 45% 30% Rising Well above the org median


Focus hours per person per week 9 12 Falling Bottom quarter


After-hours chat messages from the manager per person per week 2 1 Rising Top quarter


Reading this example: the team gets more 1:1s than the median, but its focus time is falling and its manager joins far more of its meetings than most managers do. That is the conversation to have, not the 1:1 count.


## How to set targets: your own baseline first, then benchmarks


Published benchmarks for manager metrics often have no source or come from very different companies. Set targets from evidence you can check:


- **Your own spread.** Compare each team with the organization median and quarters. A team in the bottom quarter for focus time is worth a conversation, whatever the number.
- **Trends.** A falling line matters more than a single week. Use rolling 4-week or 12-week windows to smooth out holidays and launches.
- **Comparable teams.** Compare sales managers with sales managers and engineering managers with engineering managers. Meeting patterns differ a lot by function.
- **Outside benchmarks.** Use benchmark data that names its source and splits results by role. Worklytics'[Workplace Metrics Benchmark](https://www.worklytics.co/blog/workplace-metrics-benchmark-v2-including-benchmarks-for-sales-software-engineers-line-managers-executives-and-more) includes line managers and senior leaders as separate profiles.


### One on one frequency


There is no single right number of 1:1s. A new team member or a struggling project usually needs more; an experienced team on steady work may need fewer. Rather than a fixed target, watch three things together: 1:1s per direct report, cancelled 1:1s and weeks since each person's last 1:1. The last one finds the people who are being skipped while the team average looks fine.


### Span of control


Span of control is the number of people who report directly to a manager. A manager with many direct reports has less time for each 1:1 and each team meeting, so read the coaching metrics next to it. Split the count into individual contributors and managers, because managing managers takes a different kind of time.


## Running the scorecard: monthly reviews and quarterly deep dives


- **Monthly.** Share each manager's own scorecard with them and their HR business partner. Ask one question: what is one thing to change next month?
- **Quarterly.** Look across teams. Which patterns go with better retention and engagement in your organization? Update the metric list and the example flags.
- **Use it for coaching, not ranking.** A scorecard used to punish managers will be gamed: a manager can hit a 1:1 count with ten-minute meetings.


For ways to help managers improve once you see the gaps, see[how to improve manager effectiveness](https://www.worklytics.co/blog/how-to-improve-manager-effectiveness) .


## Privacy and trust


Measure teams, not individuals, and never use message or document content. Worklytics strips personal identifiers when data is first collected, shows results only for groups with at least 8 people and does not process or store any work or message content, as its[privacy page](https://www.worklytics.co/privacy) explains. Tell managers what is measured and why before the first scorecard goes out.

The manager metrics in the table above, including manager 1:1s, cancelled 1:1s, weeks since the last 1:1, manager and skip-level co-attendance, after-hours messages from the manager, focus and fragmented hours, collaboration with other groups and span of control, are part of its metric catalog. ## Frequently Asked Questions


### What metrics should be on a manager effectiveness scorecard?


Start with manager 1:1s per direct report, cancelled 1:1s, how often the manager joins team members' meetings, team focus time, after-hours messages from the manager and collaboration with other groups. Add retention and engagement as outcome measures, so you can check which habits matter in your organization.


### What is a management scorecard?


A management scorecard is a short set of measures, shown side by side for each manager or team, that tracks how a manager supports the team: how often they coach, how they protect the team's time and how they connect it to the rest of the company. It keeps the measures separate instead of blending them into one score.


### Are there industry benchmarks for manager effectiveness metrics?


Be careful with published figures: many have no source. The most reliable comparison is your own organization's median and quartiles, by function, over time. Benchmark data from a vendor that collects manager metrics across many companies can add an outside view.


### How often should managers have 1:1s with direct reports?


There is no single right number; it depends on the role and the team. Many teams aim for weekly or every other week. Track the count per direct report, cancellations and weeks since the last 1:1, and look for people who are being skipped.


### Should a manager scorecard be used in performance reviews?


It works best as a coaching tool. Share it with the manager first and agree on one change at a time. If the scorecard decides ratings or pay, managers will work on the numbers instead of the habits behind them.
